subtopic_detail: reviewing an established anticonvulsant mood stabiliser when a woman of reproductive age discloses she is no longer using contraception
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar in a community clinic reviewing a 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder. She has taken sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for four years and has had no mood episode in three years, having previously had two manic admissions.

Today she tells you she stopped her oral contraceptive three months ago because she and her partner would like to start a family within the year, and she has not told anyone at the service. She has had no mood symptoms, sleeps well and is working. She takes no other medication and no folate supplement. Her last menstrual period was two weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test in clinic today is negative. She asks whether she should just keep taking the valproate until she actually falls pregnant and then stop it.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic, no psychomotor change, insight preserved
data_table.Investigations: Urine pregnancy test negative today, full blood count and liver function within normal limits
data_table.Medication and history: Sodium valproate 1000 mg daily for 4 years, no mood episode for 3 years, two previous manic admissions, contraception ceased 3 months ago, no folate supplement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue valproate and restart reliable contraception, deferring pregnancy until the illness is longer in remission
options.rationale: Requiring a longer remission before allowing a pregnancy substitutes the clinician's preference for the patient's reproductive decision when a safer alternative regimen exists. Reliable contraception is genuinely needed while she remains on valproate, but as a bridge during the switch rather than as the plan itself. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Cease valproate today and manage her without any mood stabiliser while she tries to conceive
options.rationale: Stopping a mood stabiliser without replacing it exposes a woman with two previous manic admissions to relapse during pregnancy and the postpartum, which is itself the period of highest risk in bipolar disorder. Untreated illness in pregnancy carries its own harms and is not the safe option it appears to be. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Plan a switch to a mood stabiliser suitable in pregnancy and start high dose folate now
options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of any mood stabiliser, with major congenital malformation in roughly 10 per cent and neurodevelopmental impairment in around 30 to 40 per cent of exposed children, and the neural tube closes by day 28 when many pregnancies are not yet recognised. Switching must therefore be planned before conception rather than at a positive test, with high dose folate started in advance and the transition made slowly while she is euthymic. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue valproate and stop it as soon as a pregnancy test becomes positive, with folate then
options.rationale: This is the plan she proposes and it fails on timing, because neural tube closure is complete before a missed period is usually investigated and the damage is already done by the time a test turns positive. Abrupt cessation at that point also risks a manic relapse in the first trimester. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Continue valproate at a reduced dose of 500 mg daily with high dose folate supplementation
options.rationale: Teratogenic risk falls with dose but does not disappear below any safe threshold, and folate supplementation has not been shown to prevent valproate associated malformations in the way it prevents idiopathic neural tube defects. Halving the dose also risks losing the prophylaxis that has held her well for three years. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Valproate is effective in bipolar disorder but is the most teratogenic of the mood stabilisers, and regulatory authorities in Australia and internationally now require that it not be used in women of childbearing potential unless other options have failed and a pregnancy prevention framework is in place. Exposure in the first trimester produces neural tube defects, cardiac and craniofacial malformations, and limb defects, with an absolute major malformation rate around 10 per cent, and in utero exposure also lowers childhood cognitive scores and raises autism spectrum diagnosis rates. The practical problem is that roughly half of pregnancies are unplanned and the neural tube closes by day 28, so a plan that begins at a positive pregnancy test is always too late. Lithium is generally preferred for a woman with predominantly manic illness, with a small absolute increase in cardiac malformation risk that is far lower than valproate's, while lamotrigine suits predominantly depressive illness. Any switch is made while the patient is well, slowly, with contraception maintained until it is complete.
key_points: Valproate exposure in pregnancy causes major malformation in about 10 per cent and neurodevelopmental harm in 30 to 40 per cent.
The neural tube closes by day 28, before most pregnancies are recognised, so switching must precede conception.
Risk falls with dose but no safe threshold exists, and folate does not abolish the teratogenic effect.
Lithium suits predominantly manic illness in pregnancy; lamotrigine suits predominantly depressive illness.
Maintain contraception throughout the switch and complete it while the patient is euthymic.
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine clearance rises sharply through pregnancy because of oestrogen induced glucuronidation, so levels can fall by half by the third trimester and the dose must be raised during pregnancy and then reduced within days of birth to avoid toxicity.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: selecting parenteral sedation for escalating aggression after verbal measures and oral medication have been refused
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a metropolitan department at 1 am. A 32-year-old man brought in by police is pacing the assessment area, shouting at staff, and has just kicked a trolley across the corridor. Two security officers are present and the area has been cleared of other patients.

De-escalation has been attempted for 20 minutes by an experienced nurse and he has twice refused oral olanzapine wafers. Collateral from police is that he has been using methamphetamine over the past three days and has no known medical history. He is not obviously intoxicated with alcohol and there is no smell of alcohol on his breath. His observations were obtained briefly during a calmer moment and his blood glucose is 6.8 mmol/L. A twelve lead electrocardiogram has not been possible and there is no previous record in the hospital system. He now advances towards a nurse with a clenched fist.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, blood pressure 148/86, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Agitated and pacing, dilated pupils, no focal neurological signs, no head injury evident, no smell of alcohol
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 6.8 mmol/L, no electrocardiogram obtainable, no previous hospital record
data_table.Measures attempted: 20 minutes of verbal de-escalation, oral olanzapine wafer refused twice, area cleared, security present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological management now?

options.text: Midazolam 10 mg intramuscularly repeated at 10 minute intervals until sedation is achieved
options.rationale: Midazolam works quickly but produces more respiratory depression and more frequent need for airway intervention than droperidol, and an open ended repeat schedule compounds that risk. It is a reasonable adjunct where a single agent has failed, which is the near pair distinction between adjunctive and first line use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Withhold sedation until an electrocardiogram can be obtained to exclude a prolonged QT interval
options.rationale: Waiting for a tracing that cannot be obtained in an actively assaultive patient leaves staff at risk and delays treatment indefinitely. Australian emergency data have shown that droperidol at these doses does not produce clinically significant QT related events, which is why a pre-sedation electrocardiogram is not a prerequisite in this setting. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

options.text: Ketamine 4 mg/kg intramuscularly as a single dose with anaesthetic support on standby
options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved as a rescue agent for severe disturbance that has failed conventional sedation, because it carries higher rates of intubation, laryngospasm and emergence phenomena. Using it before a first line agent has been tried escalates risk without evidence of benefit. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

options.text: Droperidol 10 mg intramuscularly with continuous monitoring once restraint is established
options.rationale: Droperidol given intramuscularly is the agent supported by the largest Australian emergency department trials for acute behavioural disturbance, achieving sedation faster and with fewer additional doses than benzodiazepine monotherapy, and its cardiac safety at these doses has been demonstrated prospectively. Continuous monitoring after administration is part of the intervention rather than an optional extra, because the main risks are over sedation and airway compromise. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg orally offered again with a further period of verbal de-escalation
options.rationale: Oral medication requires cooperation he has already twice declined, and diazepam has a slow and unpredictable onset by mouth, so this leaves a nurse exposed to imminent assault. Continued de-escalation is correct until the point of physical threat, which has now been crossed. (Source: ACEM: Acute Behavioural Disturbance Guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute behavioural disturbance is managed along a graded pathway that begins with environmental measures and verbal de-escalation, moves to offered oral medication, and reaches parenteral sedation with physical restraint only when there is an immediate risk to the patient or others. Australian emergency medicine research, particularly the work underpinning current practice, established droperidol as an effective and safe first line parenteral agent and overturned an earlier international withdrawal driven by concerns about QT prolongation. Sedation is a high risk intervention in its own right, so continuous observation with pulse oximetry, regular vital signs and airway readiness is mandatory afterwards, and the duration of any restraint must be the minimum necessary and fully documented. Every episode requires consideration of the medical differential, since hypoglycaemia, head injury, hypoxia, sepsis, delirium and drug intoxication or withdrawal all present with agitation. A debrief with the patient and with staff afterwards is part of the standard, as is review of whether the legal framework used was appropriate.
key_points: De-escalation and offered oral medication precede parenteral sedation wherever it is safe to attempt them.
Droperidol intramuscularly is the first line parenteral agent in Australian emergency practice.
Continuous monitoring after sedation is mandatory, with over sedation and airway compromise the main risks.
Exclude hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury and sepsis as causes of agitation in every case.
Restraint must be for the shortest necessary period, documented, and followed by a debrief.
explanation.pearls: Check a blood glucose before or immediately alongside sedation in every agitated patient, since hypoglycaemia is the one cause of acute behavioural disturbance that sedation alone will convert from reversible into fatal.

subtopic_detail: selecting first line treatment for involuntary movements and vocalisations in an adolescent whose school is demanding they be stopped
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 13-year-old boy whose school has written asking that his shoulder shrugging, eye blinking and repeated throat clearing be stopped because they disrupt the classroom.

His mother says the movements began when he was 7, that different ones come and go over months, and that they are worse when he is tired or anxious about a test and almost absent when he is absorbed in building models. He tells you he can hold them back for a while in class but that the urge builds like a sneeze until he has to let it out, and that holding them in is exhausting. He has no compulsions performed to prevent a feared outcome and no obsessional thoughts. He is doing well academically, has friends, and finds the movements themselves only mildly bothersome. He is otherwise well and takes no medication.

data_table.Examination: Brief repetitive shoulder shrugging, eye blinking and throat clearing observed during the consultation, suppressible on request with subsequent rebound, no chorea, normal tone, power and coordination
data_table.History: Onset at age 7 with a waxing and waning course over more than 12 months, preceded by a build up of urge, worse with fatigue and anxiety
data_table.Negative findings: No obsessions or compulsions, no academic or social impairment, only mild distress from the movements themselves

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line management?

options.text: Commence risperidone at a low dose and titrate against the frequency of the movements
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do reduce tic severity and are used when tics cause pain, injury or substantial impairment, but they bring weight gain, metabolic change and extrapyramidal effects to a boy whose tics bother his school more than they bother him. Treating to satisfy an external complaint rather than the patient's own impairment is the anti-pattern here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor to target the underlying compulsive behaviour
options.rationale: These agents treat the obsessive compulsive disorder that frequently coexists with tic disorders, which makes this a genuine near pair, but a compulsion is performed to neutralise an obsessional thought whereas his movements follow a physical premonitory urge. He has no obsessions on direct questioning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise him to suppress the movements in class and reward successful suppression at home
options.rationale: Suppression without a substitute response is effortful and followed by a rebound increase, so a reward programme built on it sets him up to fail and adds shame to the picture. Habit reversal differs precisely in that it supplies a competing movement to perform when the urge arrives. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and testing for antistreptolysin O titre
options.rationale: Investigation is reserved for atypical features such as abrupt onset, a fixed rather than migrating pattern, or abnormal neurological signs, none of which he has after six years of a classical waxing and waning course. A raised streptococcal titre is common in healthy children and would generate uncertainty rather than resolve it. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

options.text: Refer for comprehensive behavioural intervention with habit reversal training and psychoeducation
options.rationale: Behavioural therapy built around habit reversal is first line for tic disorders where the tics themselves cause limited impairment, and it teaches a competing response to the premonitory urge rather than attempting suppression. Psychoeducation directed at the school is an essential part of it, because demands to stop the tics increase anxiety and therefore tic frequency. (Source: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance)
source_refs: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

explanation.summary: Tic disorders affect roughly 1 per cent of school aged children, with Tourette syndrome requiring multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic present for more than a year with onset before age 18. The features that distinguish tics from other movement disorders are the premonitory urge, temporary suppressibility with rebound, a waxing and waning course over months, and variation with fatigue, excitement and anxiety. Severity typically peaks in early adolescence and improves substantially through the late teens in the majority, which is an important part of what families are told. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder coexist in a large proportion and frequently cause more functional impairment than the tics themselves, so both are screened for in every case. Treatment is stepped, beginning with education of the family and school and behavioural therapy, with medication reserved for tics causing pain, injury, or genuine impairment reported by the young person rather than by others.
key_points: A premonitory urge relieved by the movement distinguishes a tic from chorea, dystonia or a stereotypy.
Suppression is possible briefly but is effortful and followed by rebound.
Screen every child with tics for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and obsessive compulsive disorder.
Severity usually peaks in early adolescence and improves through the late teens.
Treat the impairment the young person reports, not the disruption reported by others.
explanation.pearls: Habit reversal works by pairing awareness training with a competing response that is physically incompatible with the tic and held for about a minute until the urge subsides, which is why it succeeds where simple instruction to stop reliably fails.

sources.label: RANZCP: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Guidance

subtopic_detail: responding to new agitation in residential care when an antipsychotic is requested and a reversible precipitant has not been sought
stem:
You are the general practitioner attending a residential aged care facility. Staff ask you to prescribe risperidone for an 82-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease who has become agitated and resistive over the past five days, shouting during personal care and pushing a carer's hand away during showering.

He has lived there for two years with no previous behavioural concerns and no history of aggression. Staff say the behaviour happens almost entirely during showering and toileting and that he settles within minutes once left alone in his chair. They report he has been eating less and that his urine has smelled strong, although a dipstick two days ago showed leucocytes with no nitrites and he has no fever or dysuria. He started oxybutynin three weeks ago for urinary frequency, prescribed by a locum. His usual medications are donepezil, perindopril and atorvastatin.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, blood pressure 126/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Calm when seated, distressed only during personal care, dry mouth, abdomen soft with a fullness suprapubically, no guarding
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick two days ago with leucocytes and no nitrites, no fever or dysuria
data_table.Medications: Donepezil, perindopril, atorvastatin, and oxybutynin started 3 weeks ago for urinary frequency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Assess for a reversible precipitant including urinary retention and review the oxybutynin
options.rationale: New behaviour change in established dementia is treated as a symptom with a cause, and the timing after an anticholinergic was started, the dry mouth, the suprapubic fullness and the confinement of distress to toileting and showering all point to retention. Anticholinergics also worsen cognition directly and oppose the cholinesterase inhibitor he is already taking, so reviewing that drug addresses two problems at once. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Start trimethoprim 300 mg at night for seven days to treat a urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Leucocytes without nitrites in an afebrile resident with no dysuria most often represents asymptomatic bacteriuria or sample contamination rather than infection, and treating it drives resistance without improving behaviour. Strong smelling urine is not a diagnostic criterion for urinary tract infection at any age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oxazepam 7.5 mg before showering to reduce distress during personal care episodes
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines in older people with dementia increase falls, fractures and confusion and can cause paradoxical disinhibition, and premedicating before care would entrench the problem rather than solve it. Timing sedation to a trigger also concedes that the trigger has not been examined. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the donepezil dose and arrange review by the dementia behaviour advisory service
options.rationale: Specialist behavioural advice is valuable and the service is a genuine Australian resource, but escalating the cholinesterase inhibitor does not treat acute agitation and the referral pathway takes time he does not need to spend in pain. The immediate task is to look for the reversible cause. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

options.text: Start risperidone 0.25 mg at night and review the behaviour after two weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Antipsychotics in dementia raise the risk of stroke and of death and are indicated only after reversible causes are excluded and non pharmacological measures have failed, usually where there is severe distress or risk of harm. Prescribing now would treat a behaviour whose trigger is identifiable and whose likely cause is sitting in his medication list. (Source: RACGP: Aged Care Clinical Guide)

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are common but a sudden change in a resident who has been settled for years should be read as a new symptom with a cause rather than as disease progression. The standard approach examines pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, drug effects, sensory impairment, and the environmental and interpersonal triggers around care tasks, since resistance confined to showering or toileting almost always signals discomfort or a sense of threat during that activity. Anticholinergic drugs are a frequent and reversible contributor, worsening cognition, precipitating retention, and directly opposing cholinesterase inhibitors prescribed for the dementia itself. Antipsychotics carry an increased risk of cerebrovascular events and death in this population, are restricted under Australian aged care quality standards, require informed consent from the resident or substitute decision maker, and should be reviewed for cessation within twelve weeks when used. Non pharmacological approaches, including changing who provides care, the time of day and the manner of approach, resolve a large proportion of these presentations.
key_points: A sudden behavioural change in stable dementia is a symptom with a cause until proven otherwise.
Screen for pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, new drugs and sensory deficits first.
Anticholinergics worsen cognition, cause retention and oppose cholinesterase inhibitors.
Antipsychotics in dementia increase stroke and mortality risk and require consent and time limited review.
Behaviour confined to personal care usually reflects discomfort or perceived threat during that task.
explanation.pearls: A bladder scan at the bedside takes two minutes and a residual volume above 300 mL identifies retention as the cause of agitation in a resident who cannot report it, which is a far higher yield first test than a urine dipstick in this setting.

subtopic_detail: deciding on inpatient medical admission for a young person with restrictive eating when the weight alone does not meet the usual threshold
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar assessing a 17-year-old woman referred by her general practitioner with six months of food restriction and compulsive exercise. She runs 12 km daily and has cut out all carbohydrate, and her periods stopped four months ago.

She weighs 52 kg at 168 cm, giving a body mass index of 18.4, but her weight six months ago was 68 kg. She is adamant she is not underweight and says her general practitioner agreed her weight was in the healthy range. She feels dizzy standing and fainted once last week while running. She is alert and engaged in conversation with no confusion. Her sitting pulse is 38 beats per minute, and on standing after three minutes her pulse rises to 62 with a fall in systolic pressure from 98 to 74 mmHg. Her potassium is 3.0 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5) and her phosphate is 0.71 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5).

data_table.Vital signs: Sitting pulse 38, blood pressure 98/56 sitting falling to 74/48 standing, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 per cent in air, temperature 35.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, cool peripheries, lanugo hair over the forearms, unable to rise from a squat without using her arms
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.0 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.8 to 1.5), magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7 to 1.1), electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a corrected QT interval of 468 ms
data_table.Weight history: 52 kg at 168 cm giving a body mass index of 18.4, down from 68 kg six months ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence fluoxetine and arrange psychiatric outpatient follow up within two weeks
options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a role in bulimia nervosa and in comorbid depression once weight is restored, but it does not treat restrictive eating and is ineffective in the malnourished state. Starting it now would also delay the medical care that her observations demand. (Source: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Arrange urgent medical admission for cardiac monitoring and supervised refeeding
options.rationale: Admission criteria in eating disorders are driven by physiological instability rather than by body mass index, and she has bradycardia below 40, a postural systolic drop over 20 mmHg, hypothermia, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia and a prolonged corrected QT interval. The rate and magnitude of weight loss, 16 kg in six months, carries the physiological risk here even though the absolute weight sits in the population healthy range. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Arrange outpatient family based treatment with weekly weight and electrolyte monitoring
options.rationale: Family based treatment is the highest evidence outpatient treatment for adolescents and will be the right framework once she is medically stable, so this is the correct destination reached in the wrong order. Outpatient care assumes physiological stability, which her bradycardia and postural drop exclude. (Source: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Replace potassium orally, advise stopping running, and review in the clinic in one week
options.rationale: Correcting a single electrolyte while leaving her unmonitored ignores the bradycardia, the prolonged corrected QT interval and the hypophosphataemia, any of which can precipitate an arrhythmia. A week is a long interval for a patient who has already fainted. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)

options.text: Reassure her that her body mass index is within the healthy range and arrange dietitian review
options.rationale: Using body mass index alone as the gate for concern is the specific error this presentation tests, and it is the reasoning that produced the earlier reassurance she now quotes back. A person can be physiologically critical at a normal body weight if the loss has been rapid. (Source: ANZAED: Eating Disorder Treatment Principles)

explanation.summary: Decisions about admission in eating disorders rest on physiological parameters, the rate of weight loss and psychiatric risk, not on body mass index in isolation, and the group most often missed is those whose starting weight was high and who therefore remain in the population healthy range after losing a dangerous amount. Cardiovascular instability is the dominant acute risk, with bradycardia below 40 beats per minute, postural drops, hypotension, hypothermia and electrolyte disturbance all indicating a need for monitored inpatient care. Refeeding syndrome follows the reintroduction of carbohydrate to a depleted patient, as insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly and thiamine stores are consumed, producing arrhythmia, cardiac failure, delirium and seizures. A phosphate already below the reference range before feeding has begun marks a patient at particularly high risk. Australian practice uses supervised refeeding with daily electrolytes in the first week, thiamine before any carbohydrate load, and the recognition that starting too cautiously prolongs malnutrition and carries its own harm.
key_points: Admission decisions rest on physiological instability, not body mass index alone.
Rapid or large weight loss carries risk even when the absolute weight appears normal.
Bradycardia below 40, postural drop over 20 mmHg systolic and hypothermia are admission criteria.
A low phosphate before feeding starts identifies a patient at high risk of refeeding syndrome.
Give thiamine before any carbohydrate load and monitor phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily.
explanation.pearls: Bradycardia in anorexia nervosa is an adaptive energy conserving response, so a pulse that rises while the patient is still losing weight signals infection or another intercurrent illness rather than recovery, and it is a more worrying sign than the bradycardia itself.

sources.label: RANZCP: Eating Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: attributing persistent psychotic symptoms between mood episodes when a stimulant history offers a competing explanation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 29-year-old man in a community clinic with two years of case notes to work from. He has had three documented episodes: two of elevated mood with reduced sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lasting about a month each, and one of depression lasting ten weeks.

The notes record that he believed a government agency was inserting thoughts into his mind during both elevated episodes and during the depressive one. He used methamphetamine two to three times a week until fourteen months ago and has provided supervised negative urine drug screens fortnightly since, with no positive result in that period.

Over the past four months his mood ratings have been consistently euthymic, his sleep has been seven to eight hours nightly, and his activity and speech have been unremarkable at every review. He nonetheless continues to report that his thoughts are being placed there by the agency and that a voice comments on what he is doing. He has taken quetiapine 400 mg at night throughout and has not missed doses on pharmacy records.

data_table.Examination: Euthymic affect with normal rate and volume of speech, no psychomotor change, thought insertion and third person auditory hallucinations described calmly
data_table.Course: Psychotic symptoms present continuously for 4 months while mood ratings have remained euthymic; three prior mood episodes each with concurrent psychotic symptoms
data_table.Substance history: Methamphetamine use ceased 14 months ago, fortnightly supervised urine drug screens negative throughout that period
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid function and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain all within normal limits

lead_in: Which diagnosis best accounts for this presentation?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
options.rationale: This cannot be correct because two discrete episodes of elevated mood with reduced sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lasting a month each establish mania, which excludes a unipolar diagnosis entirely. Mood incongruent psychosis in unipolar depression does exist but requires that no manic episode has ever occurred. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features
options.rationale: This would be the diagnosis if every psychotic symptom appeared only alongside a mood episode and remitted with it, which was true of his first two years but is not true now. The four months of psychosis with euthymic mood ratings is the finding that breaks this option. (Source: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder of the bipolar type
options.rationale: The diagnosis requires an uninterrupted period of illness with a major mood episode concurrent with psychotic symptoms, plus delusions or hallucinations for two or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, and mood episodes present for the majority of the total illness duration. His four months of psychosis with documented euthymia satisfies the second criterion, while three substantial mood episodes across two years satisfies the third. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Methamphetamine induced psychotic disorder
options.rationale: Stimulant induced psychosis usually resolves within a month of abstinence and a persisting form is described, which makes this a genuine competing explanation given his history. Fourteen months of supervised negative screens with symptoms continuing at full intensity, alongside three mood episodes, exceeds what the substance can account for. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

options.text: Schizophrenia with a superimposed depressive episode
options.rationale: Schizophrenia is diagnosed when mood episodes are absent or brief relative to the total duration of illness, and his two manic and one depressive episodes occupy a substantial proportion of two years. The distinguishing quantity is the proportion of the illness during which a mood episode is present, which is the single criterion separating these two options. (Source: RANZCP: Psychosis Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder sits between the psychotic and mood disorders and is diagnosed longitudinally rather than cross sectionally, which is why a single interview can never establish it and a documented course is essential. The defining requirement is a period of two weeks or more of delusions or hallucinations without a prominent mood episode, occurring within an illness in which mood episodes are otherwise present for the majority of the time. If psychosis occurs only during mood episodes the diagnosis is a mood disorder with psychotic features, and if mood episodes are brief relative to the psychotic illness the diagnosis is schizophrenia. Substance induced psychosis must be excluded before either, and stimulant related psychosis is a particular problem in Australian practice because methamphetamine use is common, the symptoms are indistinguishable cross sectionally, and a persisting form exists. Diagnostic reasoning therefore rests on the timeline, namely how long the psychosis has outlasted abstinence and what proportion of the illness has been occupied by mood episodes, and the diagnosis is revisited as that picture develops.
key_points: The diagnosis requires two or more weeks of psychosis without a prominent mood episode.
Mood episodes must occupy the majority of the total duration of the illness.
Psychosis confined to mood episodes indicates a mood disorder with psychotic features instead.
Brief mood episodes relative to the psychotic illness indicate schizophrenia instead.
Stimulant induced psychosis usually resolves within a month of abstinence, so a persisting picture needs another explanation.
explanation.pearls: Methamphetamine associated psychosis recurs on re-exposure with far less drug and after a shorter interval than the original episode, a sensitisation effect that makes any return to use the single strongest predictor of relapse and which should shape relapse prevention planning more than adherence to antipsychotic alone.

sources.label: RANZCP: Mood Disorders Clinical Practice Guideline
